questions.q: Banks handling lakhs of cheque and transaction records centrally typically deploy:
questions.solution: Mainframes (e.g. IBM zSeries) are built for very high-volume, reliable, simultaneous transaction processing - exactly banking, railways and census workloads.
questions.shortcut: Bulk transactions -> mainframe; raw scientific speed -> supercomputer; one appliance control -> embedded/microcontroller.

questions.q: Which of the following is a private IP address commonly used by home routers?
questions.solution: 192.168.0.0/16 is reserved for private networks - the default address of most home routers. 172.32 lies outside the private 172.16-172.31 block, 169.254.x.x is APIPA/link-local, and 8.8.8.8 is Google's public DNS.
questions.shortcut: The private trio: 10.x, 172.16-31.x, 192.168.x. Everything else is public.

questions.q: The default file extension of a workbook created in MS Excel 2019 is:
questions.solution: Excel 2007 onwards saves workbooks as .xlsx (Office Open XML). .xls is the 97-2003 format, .xlsm is macro-enabled, .ods is OpenDocument.
questions.shortcut: X = XML = 2007+ across all Office extensions.

questions.q: Who is known as the first computer programmer for her notes on the Analytical Engine?
questions.solution: Ada Lovelace wrote the first published algorithm intended for Charles Babbage's Analytical Engine, making her the first programmer. Grace Hopper pioneered COBOL and coined 'debugging'.
questions.shortcut: Ada = first program (on paper); Hopper = COBOL + debugging. Don't swap them.

questions.q: Which of the following would be the most appropriate title for the passage?
options: Gig Work: Flexibility Gained, Protection Pending
The Coming Collapse of the Platform Economy
Why Employees Prefer Offices Over Factories
How Mobile Apps Deliver Food to Millions
questions.solution: The passage's two halves: flexibility is real (para 1) but risk and legal exclusion fall on workers (paras 1–2), and rules must catch up (para 3). (b) compresses exactly this. (a) narrows to one example from the opening sentence. (c) is contradicted — the author says such work 'will grow'. (d) is never discussed; the factory comparison is about which laws exist, not employee preferences.
questions.shortcut: Title test: cover every paragraph, add nothing, no stance stronger than the author's — only (b) survives all three.
questions.passage:
The app has changed not only how we order food but what it means to have a job. Across the world, millions now earn through platforms that assign work task by task: a ride, a delivery, a design project. Companies celebrate this flexibility, and for some workers it is real — a student can drive between lectures, a parent can log off when the school day ends. Yet the same arrangement shifts nearly every risk of doing business onto the individual. The platform owns the technology, sets the price and directs the customer to the worker; the worker owns the vehicle, the fuel, the insurance and the idle hours between jobs.

Because a gig worker is classified as an independent partner rather than an employee, she generally falls outside labour laws written for factories and offices. No minimum wage applies to hours spent waiting for a request, no paid leave cushions an illness, and contributions to a pension depend entirely on what the worker chooses, or can afford, to set aside. Several countries are now experimenting with a middle category that would grant platform workers some protections without ending flexible scheduling.

Economists warn that the deeper cost may be invisible: a workforce that cannot plan a month ahead also cannot borrow, train or save with confidence. If algorithms increasingly decide who works and for how much, the question is not whether such work will disappear — it will grow — but whether the rules governing it will grow with it. Societies have rewritten labour law before, when work moved from fields to factories; the same imagination can be applied now.

questions.q:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the highlighted segment in the given sentence. If no substitution is required, select 'No substitution required'.

Neither of the two answers **were** acceptable to the examiner.
questions.solution: *Neither* is singular → **was** acceptable. 'Have been' and 'are' repeat the plural fault; the original fails agreement.

questions.q:
Choose the correct order of the parts to make a meaningful sentence.

**1.** The river had overflowed its banks. **P:** The villagers moved to higher ground with their cattle. **Q:** Water entered hundreds of homes by midnight. **R:** Rescue teams reached only the next morning. **S:** Boats carried families to temporary shelters. **6.** Life returned to normal after a week.
questions.solution: Timeline: homes flooded **by midnight** (**Q** caps the flooding) → villagers moved (**P**) → boats ferried them (**S**) → rescue arrived 'the next morning' (**R**) → normal life (**S6**). QPSR.
questions.shortcut: By-time caps the flooding; day-boundary marker ends the chain.

questions.q:
The following sentence has been divided into parts. One of them contains an error. Select the part that contains the error.

One of my friends / are going / to London / next week.
questions.solution: The subject is *one*, not *friends*: 'one of my friends **is** going'. The phrase 'of my friends' merely modifies *one*.

questions.q: Which film won Best Picture at the 98th Academy Awards (2026)?
questions.solution: ***One Battle After Another*** (Paul Thomas Anderson) won Best Picture; Anderson also won Best Director, with the film taking six awards overall.
questions.shortcut: Oscars 2026 sweep: One Battle After Another = 6 awards.

questions.q: Digboi, the site of India's oldest oil refinery, is located in which state?
questions.solution: The **Digboi** refinery in **Assam** began operating in **1901** and is the oldest operating refinery in India. Gujarat has Ankleshwar and Koyali; Mumbai High is an offshore field off Maharashtra.

questions.q: Towering gateways called **gopurams** are a characteristic feature of which temple style?
questions.solution: In the **Dravida** style the sanctum is topped by a pyramidal **vimana**, and later temples have huge **gopurams** in the enclosure walls (e.g. Meenakshi temple, Madurai). Nagara temples have a curved shikhara and no gopuram.

questions.q: Who first discovered the cell, in 1665?
questions.solution: **Robert Hooke** observed box-like compartments in a thin slice of **cork** in 1665 and called them 'cells'. Robert Brown discovered the nucleus (1831) and Leeuwenhoek first saw living cells.

questions.q: Two triangles are similar and their perimeters are $30$ cm and $50$ cm. If the area of the smaller triangle is $18\ \text{cm}^2$, the area of the larger triangle is:
questions.solution:
Side ratio $=\frac{30}{50}=\frac35$, so the area ratio is $\frac{9}{25}$.

Larger area $=18\times\frac{25}{9}=50\ \text{cm}^2$.
questions.shortcut: Area ratio $=(3/5)^2=9/25$; scale up: $18\times25/9=50$. Trap: $18\times5/3=30$ (used the linear ratio).
questions.pattern: similar triangles: perimeter ratio to areas

questions.q: Find the greatest number which divides 70 and 125 leaving remainders 5 and 8 respectively.
questions.solution:
Required number divides 70 − 5 = 65 and 125 − 8 = 117.
$65 = 5 \times 13$, $117 = 9 \times 13$ ⇒ HCF $= 13$.
questions.shortcut: gcd(65, 117) = 13. (Options 65 and 117 are the numbers themselves after subtraction — a classic trap.)

questions.q: Point $P$ is at a distance of $13$ cm from the centre $O$ of a circle of radius $5$ cm. The length of the tangent drawn from $P$ to the circle is:
questions.figure: <svg viewBox="0 0 250 175" width="250" stroke="currentColor" fill="none"><circle cx="65" cy="105" r="50"/><line x1="65" y1="105" x2="185" y2="105" stroke-dasharray="4 3"/><line x1="185" y1="105" x2="85.8" y2="59.5"/><line x1="65" y1="105" x2="85.8" y2="59.5"/><text x="65" y="105" dx="-14" dy="6" fill="currentColor" stroke="none" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif">O</text><text x="185" y="105" dx="2" dy="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif">P</text><text x="85.8" y="59.5" dx="-4" dy="-6" fill="currentColor" stroke="none" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif">T</text></svg>
questions.solution: The radius to the point of contact is perpendicular to the tangent: $PT^2=OP^2-OT^2=169-25=144$, so $PT=12$ cm.

questions.q: What is the unit digit of $1! + 2! + 3! + \dots + 50!$?
questions.solution: Every factorial from $5!$ onwards ends in 0. $1 + 2 + 6 + 24 = 33$ → unit digit **3**.

questions.q: Seven students **H, I, J, K, L, M and N sit in a row facing north. K sits exactly in the middle. I sits second to the right of K. M is an immediate neighbour of I. J sits third to the left of M. L is an immediate neighbour of K. H sits at the extreme left end and N at the extreme right end.** Who sits **third from the right end**?
questions.solution: K (4), I (6). M touches I (seat 5 or 7); J = M − 3 must exist → M = 5 (else J = 4, K's seat). J = 2. L touches K → seat 3 (5 is taken). H (1), N (7). Seats: H, J, L, K, M, I, N — third from the right = **M**.
questions.shortcut: Test the 'immediate neighbour' two ways; the impossible one falls to a fixed-distance clue.

questions.q: Two friends start from the same point. **X walks 3 km North and then 4 km East. Y walks 4 km South and then 3 km West.** How far apart are they now?
questions.shortcut: Both walkers from the same origin; subtract components, then Pythagoras (√98 = 7√2).

questions.q: Five friends **R, S, T, U and V sit in a row facing south. R sits in the exact middle. T sits second to the left of R. V sits immediately to the right of R. S sits at an extreme end.** Who sits **immediately to the left of R** (from R's own facing)?
questions.solution: Facing south, R's left is the viewer's right. R (seat 3) → T is second to R's left = seat 5; V immediately to R's right = seat 2; S takes seat 1, leaving **U at seat 4 — immediately to R's left** (viewer's right of R).
questions.shortcut: South-facing row: swap 'left' and 'right' for the people, keep the end seats as drawn.
